title: Does remembering the beloved comfort or burn?
claim: Chapter 121, the lament of those who remember, holds two opposite accounts of memory. 1201 and 1202, which Parimelazhagar gives to the man, make recollection a joy that does not fade even in thought (உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ்) and say no pain comes from thinking of the one you love. 1207, 1209 and 1296, spoken by the woman, make the same act the wound: even remembering burns her heart (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்), thinking hard on his lack of tenderness (அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து) wastes her life, and thinking alone leaves her heart there only to eat her. The verses together locate the difference in what is remembered: Parimelazhagar glosses the object in 1201-1202 as the pleasure of past union and in 1209 and 1296 as his neglect and cruelties, and Manakkudavar reads 1202 as conditional, sweet only if no pain comes from the thinking. 1215 adds that for the woman even the sweetness of seeing him, awake or in a dream, lasts only for the moment of seeing, where the man's persists in thought.
limits: These are dramatised speeches in different moods, not a doctrine the book states and then retracts. The gender contrast rests on Parimelazhagar's speaker assignments; Manakkudavar gives 1202 to the woman, which keeps the condition but dissolves the contrast. The 1202/1207 pair is already cited in thread:gender_asymmetry, which this thread does not replace since it treats memory rather than gender.

title: Who may call him cruel?
claim: In separation the woman's body is read as public testimony, and the verses dispute what it testifies to and whether she wants it heard. In 1188 she complains that the town says only that she has grown pale and no one says he has left her. Yet in 1190 she calls the name of pallor good provided people do not broadcast his unkindness (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்), and in 1236 what hurts her, more than her slackening bangles and shoulders, is hearing him called cruel (கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). The friend reads the same body the other way: in 1232 the pale weeping eyes seem to tell of the lover's unkindness, and in 1235 the wasted shoulders declare the cruelty of the cruel one; both commentators frame 1232, 1235 as the friend's blaming of the man to console her (இயற்பழித்தல்), and 1190, 1236 as her refusals. The asymmetry is exact: she herself uses கொடியார் கொடுமை of him in 1169, where the long nights outdo his cruelty, but will not accept the word from another mouth.
limits: This is a consistency in one dramatised speaker across chapters 117, 119 and 124, not a teaching stated by the book. 1188 has no aligned commentary in the corpus, so its speaker is inferred from context; and 1169 is tied to 1235 by shared phrasing alone, so its weight in the thread is the word she uses, not a link of argument.
